His saying, Most High: ﴿A questioner asked﴾. The majority read it with these two letters, sa'ala sa'ilun, and in it there are three interpretations.

The third: a seeker sought.

﴿of a punishment that will surely befall﴾. Regarding this seeker there are three sayings. The first: he was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who was the standard-bearer of the polytheists on the day of Badr, and he asked for this in his saying: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. The second: he was Abu Jahl, who was the one who said this. This was said by Rabi' ibn Abi Hamza.

The third: it was the saying of a group of Quraysh.

One: it is the punishment in the Hereafter. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: it was revealed in Makkah, and its punishment was on the day of Badr, by killing and capture. This was said by al-Suddi.

Nafi' and Zayd ibn Aslam and his son read (sa'ala sa'il) without hamza. Sa'il is a valley in Hell, and it was so named because it flows (yasil) with punishment.

﴿from Allah, Lord of the ascending stairways﴾. Regarding this there are five interpretations. The first: Lord of the degrees (al-darajat). This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: Lord of bounties and favours. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: Lord of greatness and exaltation.

The fourth: Lord of the angels, because they ascend to Him. This was said by Qutaybah.

The second: it is Jibril, as Allah Most High said: ( ﴿The trustworthy Spirit brought it down﴾ ).

The third: it is a creation of Allah's creation, in the form of humans but not human. This was said by Abu Salih.

﴿in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾. Regarding this there are three sayings. The first: it is the Day of Resurrection. This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b and al-Hasan.

The second: it is the duration of the world, the measure of fifty thousand years, and none knows how much has passed and how much remains except Allah. This was said by Ikrimah.

The third: it is the measure of the duration of the reckoning in the custom of creatures, that if some of them were to take on the reckoning of others, their reckoning would last fifty thousand years; but Allah Most High takes it up in the swiftest duration.

Mu'adh related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: ("Allah will reckon them within the time between the two prayers, and for this reason He named Himself Swift in reckoning, and the Swiftest of reckoners.")

The second: it is the patience in which there is no outpouring of grief nor complaint.

The third: it is waiting without haste, said by Ibn Bahr.

The fourth: it is courtesy in outward conduct, said by al-Hasan.

Regarding what he was commanded to be patient over there are two sayings:

One: he was commanded to be patient over what the polytheists slandered him with, that he was a madman, a sorcerer, and a poet. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: he was commanded to be patient over their disbelief, and that was before their fighting was enjoined. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

﴿Indeed they see it as far off﴾. Regarding this there are two sayings:

One: it is the Resurrection on the Day of Judgement.

The second: the punishment of the Fire.

One: it is impossible and will not happen.

The second: it is their deeming it far-fetched concerning the Hereafter.

﴿but We see it as near﴾, i.e. certain to occur, because what is certain to occur is near.

The third: it is the measure of the duration of the reckoning in the custom of creatures, that if some of them were to take on the reckoning of others, their reckoning would last fifty thousand years; but Allah Most High takes it up in the swiftest duration.

Mu'adh related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: ("Allah will reckon them within the time between the two prayers, and for this reason He named Himself Swift in reckoning, and the Swiftest of reckoners.")

The second: it is the patience in which there is no outpouring of grief nor complaint.

The third: it is waiting without haste, said by Ibn Bahr.

The fourth: it is courtesy in outward conduct, said by al-Hasan.

Regarding what he was commanded to be patient over there are two sayings:

One: he was commanded to be patient over what the polytheists slandered him with, that he was a madman, a sorcerer, and a poet. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: he was commanded to be patient over their disbelief, and that was before their fighting was enjoined. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

One: it is the Resurrection on the Day of Judgement.

One: it is impossible and will not happen.

The second: it is their deeming it far-fetched concerning the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on surah 70, verses 19–35:

﴿Indeed, mankind was created anxious.﴾ Al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: it means the disbelievers.

There are six interpretations of *al-halu* (anxious, impatient):

First: it means stingy. This was said by al-Hasan.

Second: it means greedy. This was said by Ikrimah.

Third: it means the one who is extremely distressed (*al-dajur*). This was said by Qatadah.

Fourth: it means weak. This was narrated by Abu al-Ghiyath.

Fifth: it means one who is very impatient in distress (*al-shadid al-jaza'*). This was said by Mujahid.

Sixth: it is the one about whom Allah the Exalted said: ﴿When evil touches him, he is distressed﴾, and so on [to the end of the verse]. This was said by Ibn Abbas.(p-95)

Regarding it there are two aspects:

One: when good touches him, he does not give thanks, and when evil touches him, he does not show patience. This is the meaning of the statement of Atiyyah.

Two: when he becomes wealthy, he withholds Allah's right and is miserly; when he becomes poor, he asks and insists. This is the meaning of the statement of Yahya ibn Salam.

﴿Those who are constant in their prayer﴾. Regarding it there are three interpretations:

First: they guard the obligatory prayers within their appointed times. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud.

Second: they frequently perform voluntary prayers (*al-tatawwu'*) alongside them. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

Third: they do not turn their attention (to other things) during them. This was said by Uqbah ibn Amir.

﴿And those who keep their trusts and their covenant﴾. Regarding it there are two aspects:

One: the trust (*amanah*) is what people entrust to him, that he should return it to them, and the covenant (*ahd*) is what people make a pact about, that he should fulfil it for them. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

Two: the trust is zakat, that he pays it, and the covenant is ritual impurity (*janabah*), that he performs the ritual bath from it. This is the meaning of the statement of al-Kalbi.

It may also bear a third sense: the trust is what is forbidden of the prohibited acts, and the covenant is what is commanded of the obligatory acts.

﴿And those who stand firm in their testimonies﴾. Regarding it there are two aspects:

One: it is their testimony regarding their prophets, that they conveyed the message, and regarding their nations, that they accepted or refused it.

Two: it is testimonies in preserving rights, by undertaking them when they are entrusted with them and by upholding them when they are discharged.

It may also bear a third sense: that when they witness a matter, they establish the right of Allah the Exalted in it, regarding what is good that they do and enjoin, and what is evil that they avoid and forbid.(p-96)

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on Surah 70, verses 36–44:**

﴿So what is wrong with those who disbelieve, rushing toward you, [with necks outstretched]?﴾ Regarding *muhti'in* (rushing, hastening) there are three interpretations:

First: *musri'in* (hastening). This was said by al-Akhfash (a grammarian), and the poet said:

> In Mecca is their home, and indeed I have seen them in Mecca, hastening toward the summons.

Second: *mu'ridin* (turning away). This was said by ʿAṭiyya al-ʿAwfi.

Third: *nazirin ilayka taʿajjuban* (looking at you in astonishment). This was said by al-Kalbi.

﴿From the right and from the left, in groups.﴾ Regarding *ʿizin* (groups) there are five interpretations:

First: *mutafarriqin* (scattered). This was said by al-Hasan, and al-Ra'i said:

> O Caliph of the Merciful, indeed my tribe, their chiefs have become *ʿizīn* before you.

Second: *muhtabin* (sitting with knees drawn up and arms wrapped around them). This was said by Mujahid.

Third: that they are companions and close associates. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Fourth: that they are a small group. This was said by Ibn Aslam.

Fifth: that they are circles and clusters.

Abu Hurayra narrated that "the Prophet (ﷺ) went out to his companions while they were in circles, and he said: 'What is [the matter] with me? I see you as *ʿizīn*.'" A poet said:

> We see ourselves around him while the night is dark, at his doors, in circles, in groups.

﴿On the Day they emerge from the graves, rushing,﴾ meaning from the graves.

﴿As if they were hastening to a target-stone (*nuṣub*) they race toward.﴾ Regarding *nuṣub* there are two readings (*qirāʾāt*): one with the *ṣād* sukun (sakin, unvocalized), and the other with a *ḍamma* on it.

Regarding their difference there are two views:

The first: their meaning is one and the same. This was said by al-Mufaddal and a group. According to this, there are four interpretations of its explanation:

First: its meaning is "toward a sign they race to." This was said by Qatada.

Second: "toward goals they race to." This was said by Abu al-ʿAliya.

Third: "toward their idols they hasten." This was said by Ibn Zayd, and it was said that they are tall stones they used to worship.

Fourth: "toward the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis they hasten."

The second view concerning the basis: that the meanings of the two readings differ. According to this, there are two views regarding their difference:

The first: that *nuṣub* with sukun is the goal to which you raise your gaze, and *nuṣub* with a *ḍamma* is the singular of *anṣab* (plural: *anṣāb*), which are idols. This was said by Abu ʿUbayda. The meaning of *yūfiḍūn* (they hasten) is "they hurry," and *al-īfāḍ* is hastening. From it is the saying of Ru'ba:

> They walk with us in haste upon the *īfāḍ*, cutting through the wide spaces of the desert, a dispersing rush.
